## Introduction

Skeletal muscle mass and strength decline with age, best prevented or treated with regular resistance training (RT). The decline in muscle mass and -strength advances upon reaching approximately 50 years of age and accelerates further after reaching 70, and, if left unchecked, has a high probability of leading to sarcopenia [@fragala_resistance_2019; @timmons_molecular_2016]. Muscular weakness and low muscle mass *per se* is further linked to diabetes, disability, cognitive decline, osteoporosis and early all-cause mortality, prevented/treated by either attaining or maintaining a healthy skeletal muscle mass [@fragala_resistance_2019; @li_associations_2018; @scheerman_sarcopenia_2021]. Older adults are expected to gain similar benefits from RT as the young, i.e., increased muscle mass, -strength and overall physical performance [@chen_is_2023; @marzuca-nassr_muscle_2024]. To ensure maximal gains from a period of RT, the anabolic stimulus provided from exercising must be sufficient [@chen_is_2023; @marzuca-nassr_muscle_2024; @paulussen_anabolic_2021], of which training volume is a principal determinant [@schoenfeld_dose-response_2017].  

Whether the anabolic stimulus is sufficient may in part depend on how responsive aging skeletal muscle is to it. Earlier findings suggest that older adults have a less responsive skeletal muscle mass compared to young, with a lower muscle protein synthesis (MPS) response to a session of resistance exercise training (RT) or protein ingestion [@atherton_muscle_2012; @timmons_molecular_2016; @wall_aging_2015]. However, baseline levels of MPS do not differ by age, and the activity in MPS-influencing proteins (e.g. mTOR) is elevated in fasted muscle from older adults compared to the young [@hodson_molecular_2019; @timmons_molecular_2016; @markofski_effect_2015]. The increased baseline mTOR activity could represent a compensation to increased relative muscle loading due to age-related loss of muscle mass, or dysregulation of the mTOR complex [@timmons_molecular_2016]. Further, likely as a consequence of altered mTOR regulation, ribosomal gene transcription and ribosome biogenesis is reduced in older adults [@chaillou_does_2023; @hodson_molecular_2019; @timmons_molecular_2016]. The increase in ribosomal content following onset of RT is believed to provide support for skeletal muscle fibre hypertrophy, through increased translational capacity yielding a higher baseline MPS [@figueiredo_regulation_2019; @figueiredo_revisiting_2019]. Indeed, regardless of age, individuals who respond to RT exhibit an accumulation in markers of ribosome biogenesis (e.g., total RNA and/or rRNA), compared to those who do not experience benefits of RT [@hammarstrom_benefits_2020; @stec_ribosome_2016; @stec_effects_2015]. 

Given the dose-response relationship between training volume and gains in muscle mass and strength observed in younger adults [@schoenfeld_dose-response_2017], and recent findings that older "non-responders" can achieve improved hypertrophy with higher training volume [@lixandrao_higher_2024], increasing training volume may represent a strategy to enhance the anabolic stimulus and thereby support the ribosome biogenesis response necessary for adaptation. Therefore, by comparing low and moderate training-volume protocols in healthy young and older adults, we aim to; determine if there is a difference in response to RT between young and older adults; does RT volume mitigate this difference; is it reflected in markers of ribosome biogenesis. The primary outcomes for these aims will be skeletal muscle mass accretion and -strength, while we will also examine the effects of training volume on glucose tolerance, due to it connection to age-related decline [@bonomini_metabolic_2015; @north_intersection_2012; @westcott_resistance_2012; @strasser_resistance_2010].

### Study Overview

This study was conducted as an age-stratified within-participant trial employing a unilateral design. All participants performed a whole-body unilateral training program, with training protocols (low and moderate) randomly assigned to either leg/arm. The intervention lasted for 12 weeks, with 10 weeks of exercising and two weeks of testing (Figure 1). The participants exercised for a total of 24 training sessions, two sessions per week for the first five weeks, increased to three sessions per week for the five last weeks, including a taper down to two sessions for the 10th and final week. The effects of the intervention on skeletal muscle mass was measured as thigh muscle volume (MRI: baseline, post), thigh muscle thickness (ultrasound: baseline, half-way, post) and lean body mass (DXA: baseline, half-way, post). Skeletal muscle strength was assessed as peak torque with the humac dynamometer, 1RM leg-press with the Keiser Airpress and maximal voluntary bicep curl contraction with the MuscleLab system (all baseline, half-way, post). Glucose tolerance was measured by the oral glucose tolerance test at baseline and post-intervention. Molecular data was gathered via micro biopsy at baseline, after three weeks of RT (six training session) and post-intervention. All tests were performed at the same time of day (± 2hrs), and measurement of lean body mass, muscle thickness, glucose tolerance, and sampling of muscle tissue was conducted in an overnight fasted state. Participants were asked to maintain their habitual physical activity level throughout the intervention, and to not perform any additional type of heavy exercise.

All participants gave their written informed consent before study enrollment. The study was approved by the Regional Committee for Medical and Health Research Ethics - South-East Norway (ID nr. 255224), pre-registered at clinicaltrials.gov (Identifier: NCT05063279), and conducted according to the Helsinki Declaration.


### Participants

Thirty-two young (24 ± 3.1 years) and 49 old (75.5 ± 5.6 years) adults were recruited locally; 10 of the old participants were randomly allocated to a control group. Inclusion criteria were age 20–30 or above 70 years (Figure 1). Exclusion criteria were: insufficient Norwegian proficiency; RT more than once weekly and/or endurance training three or more times weekly within the last six months; unstable cardiovascular disease; illness or injury contraindicating RT; serious mental illness; or allergy to local anaesthesia.


### Resistance training protocol

Resistance training was performed as a whole-body training program. Each RT-session contained three lower-body exercises (unilateral leg press, unilateral knee extension and -flexion) and three upper-body exercises (unilateral chest-press, unilateral bent-over rows, and unilateral bicep curls), using individualized settings in all exercise apparatuses. The low training volume condition was performed as a single set of 10RM per exercise, and the moderate training volume condition was performed as three sets of 10RM per exercise. As a general warm-up, the participants cycled on an indoor exercicse bicycle for 5-10 minutes. Before lower-body exercises the participants performed 1 set of 10 repetitions in bilateral leg press, and before upper-body exercises they performed a warm-up set of 10 push-ups, modified to their individual fitness level (e.g., standard, from the knees, or against a wall). To ensure progressive loading and an adequate stimulation of the skeletal muscle, the exercise load was increased in the following set if the participants lifted more than 12 repetitions. Resting time between each set was two minutes. For safety and standardization purposes, all sessions were monitored by trained personnel. To ensure sufficient recovery, at least one day separated training days throughout the intervention.


### Measurement of body mass composition

MRI was measured in a non-fasted state, in accordance with the manufacturer’s protocol (S-Scan, Esaote Europe B.V., Maastricht, the Netherlands). The images were analysed using the 3D Slicer software (SOURCE). The layering details within 3D Slicer software were the same for all the images (fat = 300-max, muscle = 1-300, bone = 0-750, and intra-muscular fat = 300-max), as was the calculation of the area to be analyzed (approx. 20% from the trochanter major proximally and 30% from the knee-joint distally). Muscle thickness of m. vastus lateralis and m. rectus femoris were measured using B-mode ultrasonography (SmartUs EXT-1 M, Telemed, Vilnius, Lithuania) with a 39 mm 12 MHz, linear array probe. Transverse images were obtained ~60% distally from the trochanter major towards the femoral lateral epicondyle. Three images were captured for each muscle at each time point, where the probe was relocated to the same position between each image. The position of the probe was marked on the skin and subsequently marked on a soft transparent plastic sheet superimposed on the thigh. Landmarks were marked on the plastic sheet for relocation of the scanned areas during post-training measurements. During analysis, pre and post images from the same participant were analysed consecutively using the Fiji software [@schindelin2012fiji]. The average muscle thickness of the three images captured per muscle per time point was used for further analyses. Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (Lunar Prodigy, GE Healthcare, Madison, WI, 320 USA) scans were analyzed with the manufacturer's software, where the region of interest (RoI) were matched on baseline, half-way and post images. 


### Assessment of muscular strength

After a standardized warm-up, strength assessments were performed using a standardized sequence; unilateral knee extension torque (legs), unilateral 1RM leg press, and unilateral maximal voluntary contraction in the bicep curl, using individualized settings. At each time point (baseline, halfway, post), muscle strength was assessed twice, on two separate days. During baseline testing, the first of the two testing days represented familiarisation. The participants had at least one whole day of rest between the previous training session and assessment of muscular strength.

*Knee extension torque*
Maximal isometric and isokinetic knee extension torque were measured with a Humac Norm Dynamometer (CSMi, Stoughton, Massachusetts, USA). Isokinetic peak torque was measured concentrically from 90 to 0 degrees knee angle (extended knee was set to 0 degrees) at angular velocities of 60-, 120- and 240 degrees per second, 2x3 repetitions each, with the first set of each exercise as a sub-maximal warm-up. Isometric knee extensor peak torque was measured at a knee angle of 60 degrees, for a maximum of 10 seconds and two repetitions per test. The isometric tests were concluded when the participants reached a plateau or peak torque development decreased, which on average occurred between 2-4 seconds into the test. Between sets of the same angular velocity the resting time was 30 seconds, and between angular velocities (i.e. from 60- to 120 degrees per second) the resting time was 1 minute.

*One repetition maximum*
The 1RM test was measured with a Keiser AIR300 Leg press (Keiser Corporation, Fresno, USA). As a specific warm-up, the participants performed 4 repetitions at ~50% of 1RM. Maximal one repetition leg press strength was defined as the maximal load lifted in a controlled fashion, starting from a knee angle of 90 degrees, within 5kg. From the ~50% of 1RM warm-up, the load was increased at most by increments between 10-40kg for the initial attempts, and at least between 5-10kg when the participants signified being near their maximal effort. Resting time between 1RM attempts was 30 seconds. 

*Maximal isometric bicep curl*
Maximal isometric force of the bicep muscle was measured with a MuscleLab force sensor (Ergotest Innovation AS, Stathelle, Norway), at a fixed elbow angle of 90 degrees. The participants were given one warm-up attempt per arm, and two attempts to perform their maximal force development in the bicep exercise. The isometric tests were concluded when the participants reached a plateau, peak torque development decreased (which on average occurred between 2-4 seconds into the test), or after 10 seconds.


### Oral Glucose Tolerance Test

The oral glucose tolerance test was completed in an overnight-fasted state, where participants ingested a bolus of 75g of glucose (Glucosum monohydricum, Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany) mixed with 250ml water. Capillary blood was gathered from the participants' fingers and analyzed with in-house equipment (BIOSEN, C-Line, EKF diagnostic GmbH, Barleben). The glucose bolus was ingested after the baseline blood draw, and subsequent blood draws were taken at 15, 30, 45, 60, 90, and 120 minutes after glucose ingestion.


### Skeletal muscle sampling and analyses

Muscle biopsies were collected from m. vastus lateralis. The biopsies were sampled under antiseptic and anaesthetised conditions (Lidokain 10 mg ml-1, Mylan Hospital AS, Oslo Norway), using the micro-biopsy technique with a 12-14 gauge needle (Universal Plus, Mermaid medical A/S, Stenløse, Denmark) operated with a spring loaded biopsy gun (Bard Magnum, Bard Norway A/S, Oslo, Norway). Samples were divided into four aliquots for RNA, protein, immunohistochemistry and DNA analyses. At week 3 and 12 measurements, there were 48 hours between the previous training session and biopsy sampling. 


### Protein extraction and western blotting

The wet muscle tissue was freeze-dried for 24h and dissected, then homogenised with a plastic rod in an ice cold lysis buffer. Briefly, 150ul of RIPA buffer was added per mg muscle tissue dry weight, with 1ul protease/phosphatase inhibitors per 100ul lysis buffer. The samples were kept on ice at all times except for when manually disrupting to homogenise the tissue, and then incubated for 30 min on a rotator while on ice. Following the incubation, the samples were spun in the centrifuge for 40 min, at 15 000g at 4°C. Total protein was then diluted to 2ug/ul stock and aliquoted to run the samples in triplicates for protein concentration determination and for western blotting. Protein concentration was determined in a 1:10 dilution (Pierce Detergent Compatible Bradford Assay Reagent, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Oslo, Norway).

Western blots were done using the Jess Automated Western Blot System (Bio-Techne, Minneapolis, USA), according to the manufacturer's protocol, optimized for our lab. The stock solution (2ug/ul) was prepared with fluorescent master mix from the EZ standard pack (Bio-Techne) and 0.1X sample buffer (Bio-Techne) and thus diluted to 0.75 ug/ul for the assay. The assay samples were then briefly vortexed, denatured at 95°C, vortexed and spun down prior to loading the assay plate. To control for within-plate variation, we used a total protein normalization reagent (Bio-Techne) for all assays. A specific between-plate normalization was not used, however, all samples from one participant were analyzed on the same plate. Primary antibodies were purchased from Santa Cruz Biotechnology (Texas, USA): UBF 1:50, UBF F-9, sc-13125; and Cell Signaling Technology (Massachusetts, USA): c-Myc 1:15, c-Myc D84C12. Ready-to-use secondary antibodies (anti-mouse and anti-rabbit) were purchased from Bio-Techne. After loading, the assay plate was centrifuged at 2500 rpm for 5 min at room temperature. The assay was then run on the Jess system, with the chemiluminescence detection module.

### Total RNA extraction and RNA sequencing

Total RNA was extracted using TRIzol from muscle tissue homogenised using 0.5mm RNase-free Zirconium beads (\~50 ul; Next Advanced, Averill Park, NY, USA) and mechanical agitation (Bullet Blender, Next Advanced, Averill Park, NY, USA). Chloroform (Sigma-Aldrich, Oslo, Norway) was used for phase separation, and the RNA pellet was precipitated with isopropanol (VWR International, Oslo, Norway). For assessment of RNA content and purity, RNA was eluted in TE buffer (1:2) and assessed via spectrophotometry. Samples with a 260/280 ratio below 1.8 were excluded. The RNA stock was stored at -80°C until further analyses.

`r nsamp` total RNA samples were selected for RNA-sequencing analysis of which `r nsamp_included` samples passed initial quality assessment (RIN > 8) and were used in downstream analyses. The samples were selected from the pool of intervention participants that had both baseline and post samples collected. Purified mRNA (poly-T oligo-attached magnetic beads) was used for library preparation and subsequent 150-bp paired-end sequencing (Illumina NovaSeq, Novogene Europe, Cambridge, United Kingdom). Raw reads were filtered (SOFTWARE, settings) and aligned to the Human genome (Release) followed by gene and transcript level quantification using RSEM (version).

Gene counts (filtered for low-abundance targets) were modeled using a regularized negative binomial generalized linear mixed model [@glmmmtb] including model parameters for sex, time (baseline and post-intervention), age-group (young and old) and condition (low- and moderate-volume) and the interaction between time age and condition. A varying intercept (random effect) was used for participant, and the dispersion parameter was estimated using the `nbinom2` parameterization available in `glmmTMB`[@glmmmtb]. The effective library size [@robinson2010;@edger] was included as an offset to account for sequencing depth. Regularization through an empirical Bayes shrinkage approach[@efron2010] was achieved using a two-step approach. First, naive models were fitted for all target counts (gene/transcript) using our in-house pipeline [@seqwrap] and estimates for all model parameters (except the intercept) were used to create priors for subsequent informed models. Fixed effect priors were constructed using a normal distribution with mean and standard deviations from each parameter value from the first model pass, the prior for the varying intercepts were constructed using a gamma distribution with the shape parameter informed by the mean from the naive model estimates and the  scale parameter fixed to 2. Finally, the dispersion parameter priors were constructed by fitting a trend model (Local Polynomial Regression Fit) to the association between raw mean log counts and log dispersion across all targets. The predicted dispersion at target-specific raw mean log count was used as the mean and the model residual standard error was used as the standard deviation to define a normally distributed target-specific prior.


### Statistical analyses

All statistical analyses were performed in R (version 4.5.1; R Core Team, 2025), and except for RNA sequencing, all outcomes were analysed with Bayesian multilevel models in brms [version 2.23.0;@brms], and contrasts were derived from posterior draws with marginaleffects [version 0.32.0;@marginaleffects]. Muscle volume, muscle thickness, upper-body lean mass, 1RM leg press, bicep curl MVC, UBF and c-Myc were log-transformed and standardized. For these outcomes, each combination of allocation, age group, volume condition and sex was given its own baseline and change over time. Varying effects accounted for participants (intercept and change over time) and for limbs within participants, with additional terms for repeated tests where these were performed. Peak torque was modelled as a quadratic function of angular velocity. Total RNA was modelled at the level of technical replicates, with tissue weight as a covariate. OGTT glucose was modelled as a B-spline function of sampling time. Weakly informative priors were used throughout and checked by prior predictive simulation. Convergence was assessed by R-hat (< 1.01) and effective sample size (> 400). Group changes were averaged across sexes with equal weight. They were back-transformed and reported as percent change, with between-group contrasts reported as ratios expressed in percent. Estimates are given as posterior means with 95% equal-tailed credible intervals (CI) and the posterior probability of an effect in the direction of the estimate (P(>0) or P(<0))<!-- Evidence for all other effects was described from the posterior probability in the direction of the estimate: P(>0), the probability that the effect is positive, for positive estimates, and P(<0), the probability that it is negative, for negative estimates.-->. Effects were termed credible when the 95% CI excluded zero. Otherwise they were described as likely (P ≥ 90%), weak evidence (P ≥ 75%) or no evidence (P < 75%). RNA-seq counts were modelled with negative binomial mixed models (glmmTMB [@glmmmtb]) regularized by empirical Bayes priors [@seqwrap; @efron2010]. Values are given to one decimal place, or two where rounding would give 0.0%. P-values were adjusted with the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure within each contrast (FDR < 5%), followed by rank-based gene-set enrichment analysis [@xu2024a]. Full model specifications are given in the Supplementary Material.

### Exercise Volume Load

Moderate volume exercise was estimated to ~2.8× higher than low in both age groups (young mod: 137438.7 ± 54491.7 kg, young low: 50693.5 ± 25707.7 kg, old mod: 118124.8 ± 38224.6 kg, old low: 42134.1 ± 14352.5 kg). 

### Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy

### Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy

_Thigh Muscle Volume_
Older adults in the intervention group (averaged across volume conditions) increased muscle volume by 3.7% (95% CI [1.8%, 5.8%], P(>0) > 99.9%), while there was no evidence of a change in the control group (0.0%, 95% CI [−3.0%, 3.1%], P(<0) = 50.0%). The difference between them was 3.8% (95% CI [0.04%, 7.6%], P(>0) = 97.6%). Young adults (averaged across volume conditions) increased by 6.0% (95% CI [3.9%, 8.1%], P(>0) > 99.9%), likely more than older adults, although the 95% CI included zero (2.2%, 95% CI [−0.5%, 5.0%], P(>0) = 94.0%). Within young adults, low-volume training increased muscle volume by 5.0% (95% CI [2.9%, 7.2%], P(>0) > 99.9%) and moderate-volume training by 7.0% (95% CI [4.9%, 9.2%], P(>0) > 99.9%), with a larger increase under moderate volume (1.9%, 95% CI [0.9%, 2.8%], P(>0) > 99.9%). In older adults, low-volume training increased muscle volume by 2.9% (95% CI [1.0%, 5.0%], P(>0) = 99.9%) and moderate-volume training by 4.6% (95% CI [2.6%, 6.6%], P(>0) > 99.9%), again with a larger increase under moderate volume (1.6%, 95% CI [0.6%, 2.5%], P(>0) = 99.9%). There was no evidence that the volume effect differed between age groups (0.3%, 95% CI [−1.0%, 1.6%], P(>0) = 68.5%).


_M. Vastus Lateralis Thickness_
Older adults in the intervention group (averaged across volume conditions) increased muscle thickness by 7.6% from baseline to post (95% CI [3.5%, 11.9%], P(>0) > 99.9%), while there was only weak evidence of an increase in the control group (3.4%, 95% CI [−3.3%, 10.5%], P(>0) = 83.4%). There was also only weak evidence of a difference between them (4.2%, 95% CI [−3.7%, 12.4%], P(>0) = 84.8%). By the half-way point, the intervention group had increased by 5.3% (95% CI [1.2%, 9.4%], P(>0) = 99.7%), with weak evidence of an increase in the control group (3.6%, 95% CI [−3.7%, 11.0%], P(>0) = 82.7%) and no evidence of a difference between them (1.8%, 95% CI [−5.9%, 10.4%], P(>0) = 66.0%). Young adults (averaged across volume conditions) increased by 10.5% (95% CI [6.5%, 14.9%], P(>0) > 99.9%), with weak evidence of a larger increase than in older adults (2.8%, 95% CI [−2.7%, 8.6%], P(>0) = 83.8%). The same was true at the half-way point (young: 8.9%, 95% CI [4.7%, 13.2%], P(>0) > 99.9%; difference: 3.5%, 95% CI [−2.1%, 9.4%], P(>0) = 88.7%). Within young adults, low-volume training increased muscle thickness by 9.0% (95% CI [3.8%, 14.2%], P(>0) > 99.9%) and moderate-volume training by 12.1% (95% CI [7.0%, 17.5%], P(>0) > 99.9%), with weak evidence of a larger increase under moderate volume (2.9%, 95% CI [−2.6%, 8.7%], P(>0) = 83.9%). In older adults, moderate-volume training increased muscle thickness by 12.2% (95% CI [6.7%, 17.7%], P(>0) > 99.9%), whereas there was only weak evidence of an increase with low-volume training (3.2%, 95% CI [−1.8%, 8.2%], P(>0) = 89.8%). The increase was larger under moderate volume (8.8%, 95% CI [2.9%, 14.9%], P(>0) = 99.8%). The same pattern was present at the half-way point, with weak evidence of a larger increase under moderate volume in young adults (3.3%, 95% CI [−2.1%, 8.9%], P(>0) = 88.4%) and a larger increase under moderate volume in older adults (7.3%, 95% CI [1.6%, 13.0%], P(>0) = 99.7%). The volume effect was likely larger in older than in young adults at post, although the 95% CI included zero (−5.4%, 95% CI [−12.7%, 2.4%], P(<0) = 91.9%), with weak evidence at the half-way point (−3.6%, 95% CI [−10.7%, 3.8%], P(<0) = 84.0%).

_Upper body lean mass_
Older adults in the intervention group (averaged across volume conditions) tended to increase upper-body lean mass by 1.2% from baseline to post (95% CI [−0.3%, 2.7%], P(>0) = 93.4%). There was no evidence of a change in the control group (0.8%, 95% CI [−1.9%, 3.6%], P(>0) = 72.8%) and no evidence of a difference between the groups (0.3%, 95% CI [−2.8%, 3.5%], P(>0) = 57.8%). At the half-way point, there was weak evidence of an increase in the intervention group (0.7%, 95% CI [−0.5%, 2.0%], P(>0) = 86.8%) and weak evidence of a decrease in the control group (−0.8%, 95% CI [−3.1%, 1.6%], P(<0) = 75.6%), with weak evidence of a difference between them (1.6%, 95% CI [−1.1%, 4.3%], P(>0) = 87.8%). Young adults (averaged across volume conditions) increased upper-body lean mass by 3.1% (95% CI [1.5%, 4.8%], P(>0) > 99.9%), likely more than older adults, although the 95% CI included zero (1.9%, 95% CI [−0.2%, 4.2%], P(>0) = 95.5%). At the half-way point, young adults tended to have increased (1.3%, 95% CI [−0.1%, 2.7%], P(>0) = 96.6%), with no evidence of a difference from older adults (0.6%, 95% CI [−1.3%, 2.5%], P(>0) = 74.1%). Within young adults, low-volume training increased upper-body lean mass by 3.3% (95% CI [1.3%, 5.3%], P(>0) > 99.9%) and moderate-volume training by 2.9% (95% CI [0.9%, 4.9%], P(>0) = 99.8%), with no evidence of a difference between them (−0.4%, 95% CI [−2.7%, 1.9%], P(<0) = 63.1%). In older adults, there was weak evidence of an increase with low-volume training (1.1%, 95% CI [−0.7%, 3.0%], P(>0) = 89.4%), and moderate-volume training likely increased it (1.2%, 95% CI [−0.6%, 3.1%], P(>0) = 90.0%), with no evidence of a difference between them (0.1%, 95% CI [−1.9%, 2.2%], P(>0) = 52.0%). There was no evidence of a volume difference at the half-way point in either young (−0.2%, 95% CI [−2.5%, 2.0%], P(<0) = 57.5%) or older adults (−0.6%, 95% CI [−2.7%, 1.4%], P(<0) = 71.8%). There was also no evidence that the volume effect differed between age groups (half-way point: 0.4%, 95% CI [−2.6%, 3.6%], P(>0) = 59.5%; post: −0.4%, 95% CI [−3.4%, 2.6%], P(<0) = 61.6%).


### Skeletal Muscle Strength

```{r}
#| label: fig-force-velocity
#| fig-cap: "Model-predicted peak isokinetic and isometric torque as a function of angular velocity (force–velocity relationship) in young and older adults across the resistance-training intervention. Lines show posterior median predictions from the Bayesian multilevel model, colored by training volume (low/moderate) and styled by timepoint (pre/mid/post). Top left: young intervention participants. Top right: older intervention participants. Bottom left: older passive control. Bottom right: pooled contrasts (intervention vs. control, and young vs. old, both pooled across volume condition) at the four tested angular velocities, shown as posterior mean change from pre-intervention (Δ, Nm) with 95% credible intervals, at the mid- and post-intervention timepoints."
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 10

readRDS(here("figures/fig-force-velocity.rds"))

```

_Isometric Force and Isometrick Peak Torque_
In older adults, peak torque in the intervention group (averaged across volume conditions) increased by 12.4%–19.0% from baseline to post, with larger increases at faster angular velocities (isometric: 12.4%, 95% CI [9.1%, 16.1%], P(>0) > 99.9%; 60°/s: 13.2%, 95% CI [9.3%, 17.5%], P(>0) > 99.9%; 120°/s: 14.6%, 95% CI [9.4%, 20.3%], P(>0) > 99.9%; 240°/s: 19.0%, 95% CI [11.0%, 27.6%], P(>0) > 99.9%). The control group also tended to increase (6.8%–9.2%), although the 95% CI excluded zero only for isometric torque (isometric: 8.6%, 95% CI [0.3%, 17.7%], P(>0) = 97.8%; 60°/s: 7.5%, 95% CI [−1.8%, 17.8%], P(>0) = 94.1%; 120°/s: 6.8%, 95% CI [−5.3%, 20.7%], P(>0) = 85.4%; 240°/s: 9.2%, 95% CI [−10.1%, 32.4%], P(>0) = 80.9%). There was only weak evidence that the intervention group increased more than the control group (3.7%–10.1%; isometric: 3.7%, 95% CI [−5.1%, 12.7%], P(>0) = 79.2%; 60°/s: 5.5%, 95% CI [−4.6%, 16.1%], P(>0) = 85.3%; 120°/s: 7.7%, 95% CI [−5.7%, 21.9%], P(>0) = 86.3%; 240°/s: 10.1%, 95% CI [−11.2%, 33.9%], P(>0) = 81.0%). By the half-way point, the intervention group had already increased by 9.9%–14.4% (isometric: 9.9%, 95% CI [6.6%, 13.4%], P(>0) > 99.9%; 60°/s: 11.0%, 95% CI [7.1%, 15.2%], P(>0) > 99.9%; 120°/s: 12.4%, 95% CI [7.2%, 17.9%], P(>0) > 99.9%; 240°/s: 14.4%, 95% CI [6.7%, 22.4%], P(>0) > 99.9%), whereas there was only weak evidence of a change in the control group (3.9%–7.6%; isometric: 3.9%, 95% CI [−4.1%, 12.4%], P(>0) = 82.4%; 60°/s: 4.9%, 95% CI [−4.4%, 14.9%], P(>0) = 85.1%; 120°/s: 6.1%, 95% CI [−5.9%, 19.9%], P(>0) = 83.4%; 240°/s: 7.6%, 95% CI [−11.2%, 30.3%], P(>0) = 76.5%). The intervention–control difference at this point (6.0%–7.3%) tended to favour the intervention for isometric torque, with weak or no evidence at faster velocities (isometric: 6.0%, 95% CI [−2.7%, 15.4%], P(>0) = 90.8%; 60°/s: 6.1%, 95% CI [−4.1%, 17.0%], P(>0) = 88.2%; 120°/s: 6.3%, 95% CI [−7.0%, 20.4%], P(>0) = 82.8%; 240°/s: 7.3%, 95% CI [−13.2%, 30.5%], P(>0) = 74.8%).

Young adults (averaged across volume conditions) increased peak torque by 14.2%–21.8% (isometric: 14.2%, 95% CI [10.7%, 18.0%], P(>0) > 99.9%; 60°/s: 15.4%, 95% CI [11.1%, 19.9%], P(>0) > 99.9%; 120°/s: 17.2%, 95% CI [11.6%, 23.2%], P(>0) > 99.9%; 240°/s: 21.8%, 95% CI [13.2%, 30.9%], P(>0) > 99.9%). There was only weak evidence that this increase was larger than in older adults (1.6%–2.5%; isometric: 1.6%, 95% CI [−1.2%, 5.0%], P(>0) = 84.7%; 60°/s: 1.9%, 95% CI [−1.7%, 6.0%], P(>0) = 83.9%; 120°/s: 2.3%, 95% CI [−2.4%, 7.5%], P(>0) = 82.4%; 240°/s: 2.5%, 95% CI [−4.4%, 10.1%], P(>0) = 75.2%). The pattern was similar at the half-way point, where young adults had increased by 11.6%–17.2% (isometric: 11.6%, 95% CI [8.2%, 15.2%], P(>0) > 99.9%; 60°/s: 13.1%, 95% CI [9.0%, 17.5%], P(>0) > 99.9%; 120°/s: 14.9%, 95% CI [9.5%, 20.6%], P(>0) > 99.9%; 240°/s: 17.2%, 95% CI [9.1%, 25.9%], P(>0) > 99.9%), with weak evidence of a larger increase than in older adults (1.5%–2.5%; isometric: 1.5%, 95% CI [−1.3%, 4.9%], P(>0) = 83.9%; 60°/s: 1.8%, 95% CI [−1.7%, 6.1%], P(>0) = 83.0%; 120°/s: 2.2%, 95% CI [−2.4%, 7.5%], P(>0) = 81.9%; 240°/s: 2.5%, 95% CI [−4.3%, 10.3%], P(>0) = 76.1%). The age difference was confined to the low-volume condition. At the half-way point, young adults' low-volume increase was larger than older adults' at isometric, 60°/s and 120°/s (3.6%–5.6%; isometric: 3.6%, 95% CI [0.3%, 7.9%], P(>0) = 98.3%; 60°/s: 4.6%, 95% CI [0.2%, 9.7%], P(>0) = 98.0%; 120°/s: 5.6%, 95% CI [0.1%, 12.1%], P(>0) = 97.7%), and likely larger at 240°/s (6.4%, 95% CI [−2.5%, 16.5%], P(>0) = 92.0%). By post, these differences remained likely, although all 95% CIs included zero (3.3%–6.1%; isometric: 3.3%, 95% CI [−0.1%, 7.4%], P(>0) = 97.1%; 60°/s: 4.2%, 95% CI [−0.2%, 9.1%], P(>0) = 97.0%; 120°/s: 5.2%, 95% CI [−0.4%, 11.4%], P(>0) = 96.6%; 240°/s: 6.1%, 95% CI [−2.5%, 15.8%], P(>0) = 91.5%). Under moderate volume, there was no evidence of an age difference at either time point (−1.2% to −0.1%, P(<0) ≤ 66.8%).

Within young adults, peak torque increased under both low volume (16.2%–26.7%; isometric: 16.2%, 95% CI [12.2%, 20.5%], P(>0) > 99.9%; 60°/s: 18.1%, 95% CI [13.3%, 23.2%], P(>0) > 99.9%; 120°/s: 20.8%, 95% CI [14.4%, 27.6%], P(>0) > 99.9%; 240°/s: 26.7%, 95% CI [16.7%, 37.7%], P(>0) > 99.9%) and moderate volume (12.2%–17.2%; isometric: 12.2%, 95% CI [8.6%, 16.0%], P(>0) > 99.9%; 60°/s: 12.8%, 95% CI [8.4%, 17.3%], P(>0) > 99.9%; 120°/s: 13.8%, 95% CI [8.1%, 19.8%], P(>0) > 99.9%; 240°/s: 17.2%, 95% CI [8.3%, 26.4%], P(>0) > 99.9%). The increase was smaller under moderate volume at every angular velocity (moderate vs. low: isometric: −3.4%, 95% CI [−6.0%, −1.1%], P(<0) = 99.8%; 60°/s: −4.5%, 95% CI [−7.3%, −1.6%], P(<0) = 99.9%; 120°/s: −5.7%, 95% CI [−9.4%, −2.2%], P(<0) > 99.9%; 240°/s: −7.4%, 95% CI [−13.7%, −1.2%], P(<0) = 98.8%), and this difference was already present at the half-way point (isometric: −4.0%, 95% CI [−6.6%, −1.6%], P(<0) > 99.9%; 60°/s: −5.1%, 95% CI [−8.1%, −2.2%], P(<0) > 99.9%; 120°/s: −6.3%, 95% CI [−10.0%, −2.8%], P(<0) > 99.9%; 240°/s: −7.5%, 95% CI [−13.9%, −0.8%], P(<0) = 98.5%). In older adults, low- and moderate-volume training produced similar increases (low: 12.5%–19.5%; isometric: 12.5%, 95% CI [9.0%, 16.3%], P(>0) > 99.9%; 60°/s: 13.4%, 95% CI [9.1%, 17.9%], P(>0) > 99.9%; 120°/s: 14.9%, 95% CI [9.3%, 20.8%], P(>0) > 99.9%; 240°/s: 19.5%, 95% CI [10.8%, 28.9%], P(>0) > 99.9%; moderate: 12.3%–18.5%; isometric: 12.3%, 95% CI [8.8%, 16.1%], P(>0) > 99.9%; 60°/s: 13.1%, 95% CI [8.9%, 17.5%], P(>0) > 99.9%; 120°/s: 14.4%, 95% CI [8.9%, 20.3%], P(>0) > 99.9%; 240°/s: 18.5%, 95% CI [10.1%, 27.9%], P(>0) > 99.9%). There was no evidence of a difference between them at any angular velocity, either at post (isometric: −0.2%, 95% CI [−2.3%, 2.0%], P(<0) = 56.7%; 60°/s: −0.3%, 95% CI [−2.9%, 2.3%], P(<0) = 58.6%; 120°/s: −0.4%, 95% CI [−3.7%, 2.9%], P(<0) = 60.3%; 240°/s: −0.7%, 95% CI [−6.4%, 5.1%], P(<0) = 60.3%) or at the half-way point (isometric: 0.1%, 95% CI [−1.9%, 2.3%], P(>0) = 54.5%; 60°/s: 0.1%, 95% CI [−2.4%, 2.7%], P(>0) = 52.3%; 120°/s: 0.0%, 95% CI [−3.2%, 3.3%], P(<0) = 50.8%; 240°/s: −0.5%, 95% CI [−6.4%, 5.5%], P(<0) = 56.4%).

The volume effect (moderate vs. low) differed between age groups at isometric, 60°/s and 120°/s. Relative to low volume, moderate volume was less favourable in young than in older adults, both at post (isometric: −3.3%, 95% CI [−6.5%, −0.2%], P(<0) = 98.2%; 60°/s: −4.2%, 95% CI [−8.1%, −0.4%], P(<0) = 98.5%; 120°/s: −5.3%, 95% CI [−10.1%, −0.5%], P(<0) = 98.4%) and at the half-way point (isometric: −4.1%, 95% CI [−7.5%, −1.1%], P(<0) = 99.6%; 60°/s: −5.1%, 95% CI [−9.0%, −1.4%], P(<0) = 99.6%; 120°/s: −6.3%, 95% CI [−11.0%, −1.5%], P(<0) = 99.6%). At 240°/s the difference was likely, although the 95% CI included zero (post: −6.7%, 95% CI [−14.8%, 2.0%], P(<0) = 94.1%; half-way: −7.0%, 95% CI [−15.2%, 2.1%], P(<0) = 94.3%).

_1-Repetition Maximum Leg Press_
Older adults in the intervention group (averaged across volume conditions) increased 1RM leg press by 13.1% from baseline to post (95% CI [8.6%, 17.5%], P(>0) > 99.9%). The control group increased by a similar amount (11.9%, 95% CI [4.1%, 20.2%], P(>0) = 99.8%), and there was no evidence of a difference between them (1.2%, 95% CI [−6.8%, 9.7%], P(>0) = 60.6%). Both groups had already increased by the half-way point (intervention: 9.7%, 95% CI [6.1%, 13.4%], P(>0) > 99.9%; control: 7.2%, 95% CI [0.7%, 14.2%], P(>0) = 98.3%), again with no evidence of a difference (2.4%, 95% CI [−5.0%, 10.1%], P(>0) = 73.7%). Young adults (averaged across volume conditions) increased by 12.9% (95% CI [8.3%, 17.5%], P(>0) > 99.9%), with no evidence of a difference from older adults (−0.1%, 95% CI [−5.7%, 5.8%], P(<0) = 52.6%). The same held at the half-way point (young: 9.6%, 95% CI [5.7%, 13.6%], P(>0) > 99.9%; difference: −0.1%, 95% CI [−4.9%, 5.0%], P(<0) = 52.4%). Within young adults, low- and moderate-volume training increased 1RM by 12.2% (95% CI [7.1%, 17.5%], P(>0) > 99.9%) and 13.7% (95% CI [8.4%, 19.0%], P(>0) > 99.9%), respectively, with no evidence of a difference between them (1.3%, 95% CI [−3.2%, 6.0%], P(>0) = 70.4%). In older adults, low- and moderate-volume training increased 1RM by 13.0% (95% CI [8.0%, 18.1%], P(>0) > 99.9%) and 13.2% (95% CI [8.3%, 18.3%], P(>0) > 99.9%), respectively, again with no evidence of a difference (0.2%, 95% CI [−4.1%, 4.5%], P(>0) = 53.0%). At the half-way point, there was no evidence of a volume difference in young adults (0.4%, 95% CI [−4.1%, 4.9%], P(>0) = 56.5%) and only weak evidence in older adults (1.6%, 95% CI [−2.6%, 6.1%], P(>0) = 76.3%). There was no evidence that the volume effect differed between age groups, either at the half-way point (−1.1%, 95% CI [−7.1%, 4.9%], P(<0) = 65.4%) or at post (1.2%, 95% CI [−4.9%, 7.5%], P(>0) = 64.3%).

_Bicep Curl Force Developement_
Older adults in the intervention group (averaged across volume conditions) increased bicep curl MVC by 5.3% from baseline to post (95% CI [1.6%, 9.1%], P(>0) = 99.8%), while the control group decreased (−8.0%, 95% CI [−14.2%, −1.9%], P(<0) = 99.3%). The resulting difference between groups (14.6%, 95% CI [6.2%, 23.6%], P(>0) > 99.9%) was already present at the half-way point (14.1%, 95% CI [6.0%, 22.9%], P(>0) = 99.9%), likely driven mainly by the control group's decline (−11.0%, 95% CI [−16.7%, −5.1%], P(<0) > 99.9%) rather than by a change in the intervention group, for which there was only weak evidence of an increase at that point (1.5%, 95% CI [−2.1%, 5.1%], P(>0) = 78.6%). Young adults (averaged across volume conditions) tended to increase by 3.8% (95% CI [−0.2%, 7.8%], P(>0) = 96.9%), with no evidence of a difference from older adults (−1.4%, 95% CI [−6.5%, 3.9%], P(<0) = 71.1%). At the half-way point, young adults tended to have increased by a similar amount (3.8%, 95% CI [−0.1%, 7.7%], P(>0) = 97.2%), with weak evidence of a larger increase than in older adults (2.3%, 95% CI [−2.9%, 7.8%], P(>0) = 80.3%). Within young adults, low-volume training increased MVC by 6.4% (95% CI [1.2%, 11.8%], P(>0) = 99.0%), whereas there was no evidence of an increase with moderate-volume training (1.3%, 95% CI [−4.0%, 6.5%], P(>0) = 68.5%); the increase was likely smaller under moderate volume, although the 95% CI included zero (moderate vs. low: −4.8%, 95% CI [−11.2%, 1.7%], P(<0) = 92.4%). In older adults, moderate-volume training increased MVC by 6.5% (95% CI [1.3%, 11.7%], P(>0) = 99.3%), and low-volume training tended to increase it by 4.2% (95% CI [−0.7%, 9.3%], P(>0) = 94.8%), with no evidence of a difference between them (2.3%, 95% CI [−4.2%, 9.1%], P(>0) = 74.7%). At the half-way point, there was weak evidence of a smaller increase under moderate volume in young adults (−3.3%, 95% CI [−9.6%, 3.4%], P(<0) = 84.2%) and no evidence of a volume difference in older adults (1.5%, 95% CI [−4.8%, 8.4%], P(>0) = 67.2%). The volume effect was likely less favourable to moderate volume in young than in older adults at post, although the 95% CI included zero (−6.8%, 95% CI [−15.1%, 2.2%], P(<0) = 93.2%), with weak evidence at the half-way point (−4.7%, 95% CI [−13.2%, 4.6%], P(<0) = 85.0%).

### Oral Glucose Tolerance Test

```{r}
#| label: fig-ogtt
#| fig-cap: "Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) responses before and after the training intervention, by age group. Top panels: blood glucose concentrations (mmol L⁻¹) across the 2-hour sampling period, shown for pre-intervention (left) and post-intervention (right) timepoints, in young (20–30 years) and old (70+ years) participants. Shaded ribbons represent the 10th, 25th, 75th, and 90th percentiles of the posterior distribution around the mean (solid line). Bottom panel: the estimated difference in training-induced change in blood glucose (post minus pre) between young and old participants, across the sampling period. Shaded ribbons represent the 2.5th, 10th, 25th, 75th, 90th, and 97.5th percentiles of the posterior distribution around the mean difference (solid line); the dashed horizontal line indicates no difference between age groups."
#| fig-width: 7.1
#| fig-height: 7


readRDS(here("figures/fig-ogtt.RDS"))

```

In older adults, the intervention group reduced its glucose response from 76 min after ingestion until the end of the sampling window, with the largest reduction at 120 min (−0.86 mmol/L, 95% CI [−1.28, −0.46], P(<0) > 99.9%). In the control group, the glucose response likely increased, although the 95% CI included zero (peak at 52 min: 0.46 mmol/L, 95% CI [−0.01, 0.93], P(>0) = 97.1%). The glucose response was lower in the intervention group than in the control group from 38 min through 120 min (at 120 min: −0.73 mmol/L, 95% CI [−1.48, −0.02], P(<0) = 97.7%; at 38 min: P(<0) = 97.5%). Young adults reduced their glucose response from 20 to 120 min after ingestion, with the largest reduction at 58 min (−1.05 mmol/L, 95% CI [−1.44, −0.67], P(<0) > 99.9%). This reduction was larger than in older adults in the intervention group between 30 and 78 min (P(<0) = 98.6% at 30 min and 98.2% at 78 min), with the largest difference at 54 min (−0.85 mmol/L, 95% CI [−1.34, −0.36], P(<0) > 99.9%). Before 30 min, the difference pointed in the same direction but its 95% CI included zero. After 78 min, the point estimate briefly changed sign, and there was no clear age difference by the end of the 2-h window.


### Molecular

```{r}
#| label: fig-protein-rna

Panels A, C, and E: predicted values at each measured timepoint, corrected area (arbitrary units) for UBF and c-Myc, and total RNA (ng, adjusted for tissue weight). Error bars represent the 95% credible interval around the posterior mean (point and line). Panels B, D, and F: posterior distributions for five key between-group and between-condition contrasts — Old: Intervention vs. Control, Young vs. Old (intervention), Young: Mod vs. Low, Old: Mod vs. Low, and Volume effect: Young vs. Old, expressed as the ratio of change between the two groups or conditions being compared. For UBF and c-Myc, only the pre-to-week 3 change is shown, reflecting the timepoints measured. For total RNA, both the pre-to-week 3 change (grey) and the pre-to-post change (blue) are shown, per the legend. Points show the posterior mean ratio with 95% credible intervals; the dashed vertical line indicates no difference between groups (ratio = 1). Percentages indicate the posterior probability that the ratio exceeds 1 — i.e., the probability that the first-named group or condition in each comparison showed the larger increase."
