```{r}
readRDS(here("figures/fig-protein-rna.rds"))

```

__UBF Protein__
Older adults in the intervention group (averaged across volume conditions) tended to increase UBF protein content by week 3 (19.1%, 95% CI [−7.0%, 49.0%], P(>0) = 90.1%), as did the control group (24.9%, 95% CI [−15.7%, 64.3%], P(>0) = 90.8%), with no evidence of a difference between them (−2.6%, 95% CI [−33.7%, 38.1%], P(<0) = 58.6%). There was weak evidence of an increase in young adults (averaged across volume conditions; 15.7%, 95% CI [−8.0%, 44.2%], P(>0) = 88.5%), with no evidence of a difference from older adults (−1.5%, 95% CI [−29.0%, 33.8%], P(<0) = 56.8%). Within young adults, there was weak evidence of an increase with both low-volume (15.2%, 95% CI [−18.7%, 52.5%], P(>0) = 80.8%) and moderate-volume training (17.6%, 95% CI [−15.2%, 60.7%], P(>0) = 83.2%), with no evidence of a difference between them (4.4%, 95% CI [−34.0%, 54.8%], P(>0) = 53.9%). In older adults, there was weak evidence of an increase with low-volume training (27.1%, 95% CI [−13.3%, 74.7%], P(>0) = 88.9%) and no evidence with moderate-volume training (13.1%, 95% CI [−18.8%, 55.0%], P(>0) = 74.9%), again with no evidence of a difference between them (−8.2%, 95% CI [−44.1%, 41.9%], P(<0) = 67.8%). There was no evidence that the volume effect differed between age groups (20.1%, 95% CI [−39.8%, 112.3%], P(>0) = 67.2%).

__c-Myc Protein__
The difference in c-Myc (high peak) protein content between the old intervention group (averaged across volume conditions) and the control group was large by week 3 (99.8%, 95% CI [17.5%, 216.3%], P(>0) = 99.3%). This difference was driven mainly by a decrease in the control group (−34.5%, 95% CI [−56.0%, −5.5%], P(<0) = 98.6%), while the intervention group tended to increase (25.9%, 95% CI [−8.9%, 68.1%], P(>0) = 92.0%). There was weak evidence of an increase in young adults (averaged across volume conditions; 18.6%, 95% CI [−12.5%, 57.5%], P(>0) = 85.9%), with no evidence of a difference from older adults (−3.5%, 95% CI [−37.8%, 45.0%], P(<0) = 61.5%). Within young adults, there was no evidence of a change with low-volume training (4.4%, 95% CI [−30.1%, 49.1%], P(>0) = 55.2%), while moderate-volume training tended to increase c-Myc (37.3%, 95% CI [−12.2%, 106.2%], P(>0) = 91.5%). There was weak evidence of a larger increase under moderate volume (36.2%, 95% CI [−23.8%, 127.4%], P(>0) = 83.5%). The same pattern held in older adults: there was no evidence of a change with low-volume training (9.6%, 95% CI [−29.9%, 64.4%], P(>0) = 62.0%), moderate-volume training tended to increase c-Myc (47.9%, 95% CI [−4.7%, 118.4%], P(>0) = 95.5%), and there was weak evidence of a larger increase under moderate volume (41.0%, 95% CI [−24.3%, 138.0%], P(>0) = 84.5%). There was no evidence that the volume effect differed between age groups (5.2%, 95% CI [−55.8%, 114.3%], P(>0) = 46.7%).

_Total RNA_ <!-- total amount of RNA, accounting for tissue mass, but not normalizing to RNA/mg -->
Older adults in the intervention group (averaged across volume conditions) increased RNA yield by 14.1% from baseline to post (95% CI [5.3%, 23.5%], P(>0) = 99.9%). The control group tended to increase by a similar amount (13.5%, 95% CI [−4.1%, 34.2%], P(>0) = 93.2%), and there was no evidence of a difference between them (0.5%, 95% CI [−16.7%, 20.3%], P(>0) = 52.4%). The two groups differed in timing: the intervention group had already increased by week 3 (9.2%, 95% CI [1.2%, 18.2%], P(>0) = 98.6%), whereas the control group had not changed at that point (−0.9%, 95% CI [−15.1%, 15.2%], P(<0) = 55.0%). The difference between them at week 3 was still uncertain (10.6%, 95% CI [−7.0%, 30.8%], P(>0) = 87.6%). Young adults (averaged across volume conditions) increased by 11.6% by post (95% CI [2.6%, 21.4%], P(>0) = 99.6%), with no evidence of a difference from older adults (−2.4%, 95% CI [−12.6%, 9.5%], P(<0) = 65.3%). At week 3, however, young adults had increased by 17.4% (95% CI [7.8%, 28.0%], P(>0) > 99.9%), with weak evidence of a larger increase than older adults (7.4%, 95% CI [−4.5%, 20.8%], P(>0) = 88.9%). Between week 3 and post, young adults' RNA yield likely fell back relative to older adults' (−9.0%, 95% CI [−20.4%, 4.5%], P(<0) = 91.9%). Within young adults, both low-volume (15.7%, 95% CI [3.5%, 29.5%], P(>0) = 99.5%) and moderate-volume training (19.2%, 95% CI [6.4%, 33.5%], P(>0) = 99.9%) increased RNA yield by week 3. At post, the increase was 12.2% under moderate volume (95% CI [0.4%, 25.9%], P(>0) = 97.8%), while low volume tended to increase it by 10.8% (95% CI [−0.7%, 24.1%], P(>0) = 96.6%). There was no evidence of a difference between volume conditions at either time point (week 3: 2.9%, 95% CI [−10.8%, 19.9%], P(>0) = 65.7%; post: 1.1%, 95% CI [−12.6%, 17.1%], P(>0) = 56.0%). In older adults, low-volume (12.3%, 95% CI [1.0%, 24.6%], P(>0) = 98.3%) and moderate-volume training (15.8%, 95% CI [4.4%, 28.3%], P(>0) = 99.8%) both increased RNA yield by post, having tended to increase already by week 3 (low: 10.3%, 95% CI [−0.3%, 22.0%], P(>0) = 97.1%; moderate: 8.3%, 95% CI [−2.3%, 19.9%], P(>0) = 93.3%). There was no evidence of a difference between volume conditions at either time point (week 3: −1.9%, 95% CI [−14.0%, 12.3%], P(<0) = 60.4%; post: 3.1%, 95% CI [−9.9%, 17.8%], P(>0) = 67.2%). There was no evidence that the volume effect differed between age groups, either at week 3 (5.0%, 95% CI [−14.6%, 27.5%], P(>0) = 68.4%) or at post (−1.7%, 95% CI [−20.0%, 20.0%], P(<0) = 57.2%).

_RNA-sequencing_
```{r}
#| label: fig-rnaseq-combined
#| fig-cap: "Baseline and training-related transcriptional differences between age groups. (A) Baseline age differences (Young − Old): volcano plot of gene-level estimates (log₂ fold-change) against FDR (log₂ scale), with the dashed line marking FDR = 5%. Genes with the strongest evidence of differential expression are labeled. (B) Rank-based gene-set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of the baseline age contrast, showing the running enrichment score (top) and per-gene contrast effect size (z-score, bottom) across gene rank position, for three representative gene sets (oxidative phosphorylation, heterochromatin formation, complement activation, classical pathway). (C) Age × training-response difference (Young − Old): volcano plot of gene-level estimates for the interaction contrast, in the same format as (A). (D) GSEA of the age × training-response interaction contrast, in the same format as (B), for three representative gene sets (RNA splicing, angiogenesis, aerobic respiration)."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 10


library(seqwrap)
m2r <- readRDS("data-out/m2-rnaseq.RDS")
m2s <- seqwrap_summarise(m2r, verbose = FALSE)

n_diff_expressed <- m2s$summaries |> 
  dplyr::filter(term == "ageyoung") |> 
  dplyr::mutate(p.adj = p.adjust(p.value, method = "BH")) |> 
  dplyr::filter(p.adj < 0.05) |> 
  nrow()



n_sig_young_t3 <- m2s$summaries |> 
  dplyr::filter(term == "young_t3") |> 
  dplyr::mutate(p.adj = p.adjust(p.value, method = "BH")) |> 
  dplyr::filter(p.adj < 0.05) |> 
  nrow()

n_sig_old_t3 <- m2s$summaries |> 
  dplyr::filter(term == "old_t3") |> 
  dplyr::mutate(p.adj = p.adjust(p.value, method = "BH")) |> 
  dplyr::filter(p.adj < 0.05) |> 
  nrow()

n_sig_old_volume_t3 <- m2s$summaries |> 
  dplyr::filter(term == "old_volume_t3") |> 
  dplyr::mutate(p.adj = p.adjust(p.value, method = "BH")) |> 
  dplyr::filter(p.adj < 0.05) |> 
  nrow()


readRDS(here("figures/fig-rnaseq.RDS"))

```

Comparing gene-expression profiles between age groups at baseline (Young − Old) revealed marked differences, with `r n_diff_expressed` genes showing robust differences between the groups (FDR < 5%, Fig 6A/B). Rank-based gene-set enrichment analysis [@xu2024a] indicated that young participants had relatively higher expression of genes related to aerobic energy metabolism (oxidative phosphorylation) and relatively lower expression of genes related to immune system activation (complement activation, classical pathway) and epigenetic regulation of gene expression (heterochromatin formation). Training induced a large, broad transcriptional response in both age groups: `r n_sig_young_t3` genes changed from baseline to post in young participants, and `r n_sig_old_t3` in old participants (FDR < 5%, Fig 6C/D). Individual genes with the strongest training-induced changes were predominantly collagen and basement-membrane genes in both groups (e.g., COL4A1, COL4A2, LAMB1, PXDN in young; COL4A1, LAMA4, COL3A1, COL1A2, SPARC in old).

Rank-based gene-set enrichment analysis [@xu2024a] showed that the dominant biology of the training response was similar between age groups: 6 of the top 10 enriched categories were shared, with matching direction and comparable magnitude in both young and old (RNA splicing, ribonucleoprotein complex biogenesis, integrin-mediated signaling pathway, cell adhesion mediated by integrin, collagen metabolic process, and mRNA transport). Training up-regulated genes related to ECM/connective tissue remodeling (e.g., integrin-mediated signaling and adhesion, collagen metabolic process) and down-regulated genes related to RNA-processing and ribosome biogenesis (e.g., RNA splicing, ribonucleoprotein complex biogenesis, mRNA transport) in both groups. While essentially no genes (1 gene at 5% and 0 at 1%) showed a statistically significant age-dependent training response after FDR correction, gene-set enrichment analysis of the age × time interaction contrast revealed that the magnitude of the shared training response differed somewhat between age groups in specific processes: the down-regulation of RNA splicing and related mRNA-processing categories was more pronounced in young than old, while the up-regulation of angiogenesis and aerobic respiration/cellular respiration categories was more pronounced in young than old.

A smaller set of categories differed by age: young participants showed additional enrichment for cytoplasmic translation, mesenchymal cell migration, and angiogenesis, while old participants showed additional enrichment for coagulation- and vascular-related categories. In contrast to the broadly age-independent training effect, the effect of training volume (moderate vs. low) was age-dependent: a substantial number of genes differed by volume in old participants (`r n_sig_old_volume_t3` genes, FDR < 5%), while only one gene showed a volume effect in young participants. Among old participants, higher training volume was associated with relatively higher expression of genes related to mitochondrial biogenesis and oxidative metabolism (e.g., inner mitochondrial membrane organization, respiratory electron transport chain, purine-containing compound biosynthesis) and relatively lower expression of genes related to muscle contractile function and translation (e.g., skeletal muscle contraction, cytoplasmic translation, muscle organ development, striated muscle cell differentiation, ribosomal small subunit biogenesis). This volume effect was considerably more modest than the main training effect, both in the number of genes involved and in statistical strength. 


## Discussion

<!-- P1: Opening paragraph -->
Overall, old and young participants in the intervention responded in terms of muscle growth and -strength, also improving their tolerance to glucose ingestion. Weak to likely evidence suggested that older individuals in the intervention had lesser gain in muscle mass than old, and the old improved glucose tolerance less than young. In muscle strength, there were no clear differences between old and young individuals in the intervention, except that old showed no volume benefit where young showed a higher benefit of low volume for peak torque performance. Regarding the effect of training volume, old and young benefited from moderate training volume in muscle hypertrophy, but no other clear benefit from moderate training volume was found. Old individuals in the intervention increased molecular markers of ribosome biogenesis (total RNA, UBF, c-Myc) in a similar fashion to young, though on a delayed timescale, and the RNA-sequencing data showed a marked difference between age groups at baseline that became more similar after training. 


<!-- P2: Hypertrophy and strength -->

<!-- POINT 1: General expectations in young and old when exercising resistance training -->
While it has been suggested that older adults can gain similar improvements in both muscle mass and -strength as young [@fragala_resistance_2019], this was not clearly evident in the present study. The older participants likely had lesser gains from baseline to post in thigh muscle volume<!--, and upper-body lean mass--> compared to the young intervention group, a 2.2% difference, though the credible interval did not exclude zero. Thus, one cannot fully exclude a "no-difference" scenario between old and young in this regard, though it was likely due to 94% of the posterior mass favored young over old in skeletal muscle volume gains. In theory, this could represent some evidence for the "hypertrophy attenuation" in older results (~60+ years), which is now a broadly used statement [@betz_aerobic_2025; @endo_optimizing_2020; @stec_randomized_2017], despite scarce evidence of older individuals gaining less hypertrophy than the young. This hypertrophy attenuation claim likely stems from the classic MRI CSA study by Welle and co-workers [@welle_effect_1996], where they found that older individuals (62-72yrs) experienced lesser training-induced increases in skeletal muscle CSA in the elbow and knee flexors compared to young. However, the same authors also found no age-related difference in skeletal muscle CSA in the knee extensors, and the old individuals increased similarly in terms of elbow flexor and knee extensor strength, even surpassing the young in knee flexor strength increase, when strength was analysed as relative change in specific tension (strength per cm2 of CSA) [@welle_effect_1996]. Therefore, while hypertrophy attenuation was present in certain skeletal muscle, it was not universal, and despite less hypertrophy in certain skeletal muscle, older individuals had similar and even larger gains in specific tension strength [@welle_effect_1996]. Later work by Greig et al. [@greig_blunting_2011] notes the equivocal nature of the field, where some studies find less responsive skeletal muscle mass in old [@welle_effect_1996; @kosek_efficacy_2006], or similar responsiveness to young [@ivey_effects_2000]. Furthermore, recent work find no decline in the potential for muscle hypertrophy [@karlsen_preserved_2020], or no substantial influence of age on muscle hypertrophy response to resistance training [@de_santana_lower_2024]. Among the studies that have compared young and old head-to-head to this date, the results are inconclusive at best, with some finding less myofiber hypertrophy in old compared to young [@petrella_efficacy_2006; @kosek_efficacy_2006], less myofiber hypertrophy but similar strength gains [@bickel_exercise_2011; @raue_improvements_2009], or less myofiber hypertrophy and strength after 10.5 weeks, where muscle strength caught up after 21 weeks [@mero_resistance_2013]. Taken together, most studies measuring hypertrophy in knee extensors via whole-muscle volume MRI find no age effect [@welle_effect_1996; @ivey_effects_2000; @karlsen_preserved_2020; @de_santana_lower_2024], with the exceptions being the findings of Raue et al. [@raue_improvements_2009] and Welle and co-workers data on knee and elbow flexors [@welle_effect_1996]. When hypertrophy is measured on the fiber level though, this flips, and most studies find an attenuation in old compared to young [@kosek_efficacy_2006; @petrella_efficacy_2006; @bickel_exercise_2011; @mero_resistance_2013], the exception here being @karlsen_preserved_2020. In this regard, our data does not show a definitive age effect on training-induced hypertrophy, though it was more likely than not that the old intervention group increased thigh muscle volume<!-- and upper-body lean mass--> less than young. <!-- add something about the size of the changes? though credible, the changes themselves were quite small. What are other papers finding from MRI? -->

The same was not evident for muscle strength, where old increased 
Though weaker than in muscle hypertrophy, there was some evidence to suggest a possible difference in muscle strength gains between the age groups as well. Both moderate and low volume yielded increases from baseline to post in both age groups, however old control also showed strong evidence to increase isometric peak torque from baseline to post, while the other angular velocities showed weak evidence of an increase. 

Peak torque showed weak evidence of a difference between young and old, favoring young, while bicep curl MVC showed weak evidence favoring old. Further complicating this, was the weak evidence for a difference between the old intervention group and control in peak torque, as well as no difference between old intervention group and control in 1RM leg press. The difference between the old intervention and control observed in bicep curl MVC is likely due in part to the decrease in the control group, though both volume conditions showed evidence of an increase in the old, with moderate volume showing the stronger effect. Previous studies have shown differing results here, where old individuals may lag behind in hypertrophy but not in strength [@welle_effect_1996; @bickel_exercise_2011; @mero_resistance_2013] or where both change similarly [@raue_improvements_2009]. Notably, since the evidence of a difference between young and old in strength gains in the present study was quite weak, one should take care not to over-interpret it, and we cannot exclude the possibility of there not being a difference. A no-difference scenario would entail a discrepancy between muscle hypertrophy and strength gains, where the most common explanation is that neural adaptation drives the early stage strength gain, while hypertrophy is lagging behind [SOURCES]. This does not fully apply here, since both young and old had gains in muscle mass and -strength, the discrepancy stems from the young gaining more than old. Given the weak evidence of an age difference between young and old, on could argue that the old participants in the present study effectively gained similar increases in strength, with less changes in muscle mass, indeed corroborating that hypertrophy and strength does not have a 1:1 relationship. This was addressed previously by Reggiani and Schiaffino [@reggiani_muscle_2020], arguing that there are three possible relationships between size change and strength change; strength can increase in proportion to, less or more than size. At the core of this concept, lies the idea that not all muscle growth is forceful, where the proportion between sarcoplasmic proteins and myofibrillar proteins can be altered during hypertrophy, producing a higher or lower density of actual force-generating molecular motors per unit of muscle size [@reggiani_muscle_2020]. Therefore, theres no given % of CSA, muscle volume, lean mass that grant a proportional increase in the contractile machinery, some of the gain could be sarcoplasmic rather than myofibrillar [@reggiani_muscle_2020]. Alternatively or additionally, it could stem from myosin isoform shifts and post-translational changes to the contractile machinery, affecting force generation independent of size [@reggiani_muscle_2020]. Notably, myofibrillar vs. sarcoplasmic hypertrophy, myosin isoform shifts and post-translational changes are less, if at all, explored in young vs. old participants, but the notion that the skeletal muscle mass can get stronger without the same growth in size at least seems like a plausible explanation for why the old in the present study increased similarly in strength, but not size, compared to the young. Furthermore, the learning-effect should be considered, given the tendencies to increase in peak torque, and similar increase in 1RM in the control group compared to the old intervention group. The participants in the present study only had one familiarization test, perhaps not enough to rule out the learning-effect, which could explain the control groups results for lower-body strength. If that was the only explanation though, it does not make sense that the control group decreased their bicep curl MVC from baseline to post.<!-- probably need to discuss the control increase a bit more-->

<!-- Bring in the dietary aspect? This could also be mentioned as a limitation, since we have no records here ..To ensure maximal gains from a period of RT, the anabolic stimulus provided from exercising must be sufficient and ideally combined with nutritional optimisation (especially daily protein addition) [@chen_is_2023; @hamarsland_native_2019; @marzuca-nassr_muscle_2024; @paulussen_anabolic_2021]-->

<!-- POINT 2: Dose-response, low vs. moderate -->
In broad strokes, moderate-volume training was most beneficial in the hypertrophy outcomes, specifically in muscle volume, where the evidence was strong in both age groups. This remained true in muscle thickness for the old intervention group, however, the evidence was weak for the young intervention group here. No evidence of a volume-condition difference within age groups was observed in upper-body lean mass. As for the strength outcomes, there was more evidence of low-volume training being more beneficial (strong for peak torque, moderate-to-strong for bicep curl MVC) for the young, while the old intervention group showed no difference between volume-conditions. Most studies investigating the effects of training volume on muscle mass and/or -strength, tend to find that a moderate-training volume benefits both size and strength [@krieger_single_2009; @krieger_single_2010; @hammarstrom_benefits_2020; @rocha_different_2024; @chen_is_2023; @lixandrao_higher_2024], where Hammarström et al. [@hammarstrom_benefits_2020] demonstrated that young benefited more from a moderate volume in both muscle mass and strength, a contrast to our findings that low-volume training was more beneficial for peak torque, perhaps also bicep curl MVC.<!-- maybe comment this further--> A similar pattern to the present study was observed by Da Silva et al. [@da_silva_repetitions_2018], where more training volume improved hypertrophy compared to low, but no additional gain in strength/neuromuscular outcomes. @da_silva_repetitions_2018 notably only had old participants, and the volume manipulation was done through one group performing repetitions to failure, two groups performing submaximal repetitions, one of which doubled the amount of sets the repetitions to failure group had.<!-- maybe comment this further --> Further, a recent mate-regression by Pelland et al. [@pelland_resistance_2026] found a clear positive effect of volume on both hypertrophy and strength <!-- both young and old? --> (posterior probability of 100%), but also diminishing returns in both, where the diminishing returns for strength was considerably more pronounced than for hypertrophy. As such, it seems hypertrophy could be more volume-sensitive than strength, with some evidence of strength not always following hypertrophy after increasing training volume [@pelland_resistance_2026]. This could be corroborated by that strength saturates at a lower training dose, as seen when comparing; @schoenfeld_dose-response_2017, where volume reached a significant effect on hypertrophy at 10+ sets/week, against @krieger_single_2009, where strength gains only required 2-3 sets per session. Also of interest, Schoenfeld [@schoenfeld_strength_2017] found the opposite pattern when manipulating training load rather than volume, where strength was clearly load dependent and hypertophy insensitive. Furthermore, in 2019, Schoenfeld recruited 34 resistance-trained men randomized to low-volume, moderate-volum, or high-volume training, and found that while all groups experienced similar gains in muscle strength and endurance, muscle hypertrophy significantly increased with higher training volumes [@schoenfeld_resistance_2019]. Thus, one could argue that the this field is quite equivocal, but that may very well stem from the wide spread in study designs. 

Many of the aforementioned studies differ in population or duration, manipulate volume or intensity differently, or investigate old and young separately. The two studies including both young and old differ substantially in design, where one first implemented a volume/dose model in the maintenance phase [@bickel_exercise_2011], while the other manipulated training intensity rather than training volume [@letocart_muscles_2021]. @bickel_exercise_2011 recruited 39 young (20-35yrs) and 31 old (60-75yrs) untrained individuals to a 16 week progressive RT program, with a 32 week detraining/maintenance training period. In the maintenance period, one group was assigned to detraining, one group to a third of the initial volume via reduced training frequency (1 session, down from 3x/w), and one group to a ninth of the initial volume via reduced sets (1 set, down from 3) and training frequency (1 session, down from 3x/w). Following this, @bickel_exercise_2011 found similar relative strength gains but greater hypertrophy gains in young compared to old, during the 16-week training program, and also an equally sustained enhancement of muscle performance during the detraining/maintenance phase, while maintenance of muscle mass gains required more frequent dosing in the old. @letocart_muscles_2021 recruited 11 recreationally active young men and 35 sedentary old men to a 12-week resistance program where the young exercised with a moderate-load training intervention corresponding to 55% of 1RM, while the old were randomly assigned to either moderate (55%) or high-load (80% of 1RM). They exercised three times a week, with three exercises for the lower extremities. @letocart_muscles_2021 found that the old exercising with a moderate training intensity gained more m. quadriceps and m. triceps surae volume compared to the young, with no difference between old exercising with moderate- or high-intensity. Overall, our findings align with @bickel_exercise_2011 where greater hypertrophy gains were observed in young compared to old, and moderate-volume training being more beneficial in this regard, and none of these, or the aforementioned volume-manipulating studies have found low-volume to outperform moderate-volume in terms of skeletal muscle strength. This may be a novel finding, and could harken back to the pattern seen when contrasting @schoenfeld_dose-response_2017 and @krieger_single_2009, suggesting strength increases saturate at a lower training volume than hypertrophy.

<!-- P5: Glucose tolerance -->
Glucose tolerance improved more in the young compared to the old, specifically between 30 and 78 minutes after ingesting glucose. The only previous study including both young and old in a chronic RT intervention, found only nominal improvements in glucose tolerance in both groups, where elderly remained well below the young group [@craig_influence_1989]. Notably, @craig_influence_1989 had fewer participants, and compared pre-post points rather than the full time frame of the OGTT like the present study. Chronic RT studies with old adults alone have found lowered 2h glucose and OGTT AUC compared to control after 8 weeks of RT (3x/week) [@andersson_improving_2017]; decreased fasting glucose and OGTT AUC (0-30min) after high-, low- and volume-matched load for 10 weeks [@tsai_effects_2021]; decreased blood glucose, basal insulin, and HOMA-IR in postmenopausal women after 12 weeks of whole-body progressive RT [@moreno_lima_resistance_2015]; and a decrease in HOMA-IR in non-diabetic elderly men compared to type 2 diabetic elderly men and control, after 12 weeks of RT (3x/week)[@shabkhiz_resistance_2021]. Acute studies comparing single session volume effect have found reduced glucose AUC with RT, reduced fasting glucose only after higher-volume in young women [@reed_effects_2012], and improved oral glucose insulin sensitivity and glucose/insulin/c-peptide AUC in insulin resistant individuals after a high-volume session only [@silva_improvements_2026]. A meta-analysis by Li et al. [@li_effects_2021] investigated 12 RCTs with non-athletic and aged participants (60+), and found that population, training intensity, and duration all had significant effects on HOMA-IR, with largest effect sizes for high-intensity and long-term (>12 weeks) exercise in older adults without type 2 diabetes. In the same meta-analysis, they also found that moderate-intensity and short-term (<12 weeks) had a greater effect on HbA1c, particularly in people with type 2 diabetes [@li_effects_2021]. On the contrary, Zhang et al. [@zhang_effects_2025] found more inconsistent evidence for high-intensity RT, with some long-term high-intensity trials failing to improve glycemia, HbA1c, or HOMA-IR. 

Taken together, the data suggest that chronic RT should improve glycemic markers in older adults, but the effect is modest and not universal. Chronic RT improved glucose/insulin/HOMA-IR in older adults in three separate studies [@andersson_improving_2017; @tsai_effects_2021; @moreno_lima_resistance_2015], with evidence from the meta-analysis by @li_effects_2021 supporting an effect, however small on average. This is corroborated by early findings from @craig_influence_1989 and more so the present study with a high resolution OGTT curve, that elderly do indeed respond in terms of improved glucose tolerance, however less than young adults undertaking the same chronic RT. Baseline metabolic health could be a moderator of the response, but in what direction is not clear. Chronic RT did not improve HOMA-IR in diabetic elderly men compared to non-diabetic elderly men, while both groups improved strength [@shabkhiz_resistance_2021]. Acute RT, meanwhile, improved oral glucose sensitivity and glucose/insulin/C-peptide AUC only in the insulin resistant [@silva_improvements_2026]. Notably, this may very well reflect chronic vs. acute mechanisms, but with the current findings its not a clear-cut "healthier responds more" picture. In the methodological perspective of the studies reviewed here, studies using fasting glucose/HOMA-IR [@moreno_lima_resistance_2015; @shabkhiz_resistance_2021; @li_effects_2021] show less consistent findings and contradictory RT-intensity conclusions [@li_effects_2021; @zhang_effects_2025], compared to studies using outcomes derived from the OGTT [@andersson_improving_2017; @tsai_effects_2021]. Most of the methods used in these articles are collapsed to single-time point (fasting glucose/insulin, 2h glucose, HOMA-IR) or single summary statistics (OGTT AUC), which fails to capture the full window of post-prandial glucose clearance as the OGTT curve in the present study. This is important, since the difference between young and old in the present study would not have been detected by comparing for instance 2h glucose alone. Before 30 minutes, there was only a trend towards young having a larger improvement in glucose tolerance compared to the old, and after 78 min the we were no longer able to statistically distinguish any difference between the two intervention groups. The full OGTT curve also shows that not only has the old intervention group improved their glucose tolerance more than the old control group, but the difference remains credible to the last measured time point, whether the difference ends there or at a later time point however, we cannot tell.  

There might be an argument that the larger improvement observed in the young participants between 30 and 78 min is not meaningful, since the groups are statistically indistinguishable before 30 min and after 78; there's not a clear difference at the start or end of the test. However, there is evidence from cross-sectional/observational research that elevated 1-hour OGTT (>8.6 mmol/L) glucose identifies a higher-risk phenotype for future T2D and is independently associated with subclinical vascular damage and reduced insulin sensitivity/clearance, even in individuals who are indistinguishable from lower-risk individuals by standard fasting and 2h criteria [@marini_decreased_2013; @sciacqua_association_2012]. While this evidence concerns absolute 1h glucose level in cross-sectional cohorts rather than training-induced change, it indicates this region of the curve is not physiologically inert simply because it's invisible to standard fasting/2h criteria — though no comparable study has yet tested whether a training-induced improvement here confers the same protective association. It should also be noted here that while the appropriate RT volume could be an important lever [@li_effects_2021; @zhang_effects_2025], this was not testable in the present study since the volume conditions were done within-participant.

<!-- P4: Ribosome biogenesis - RNA, UBF, cMyc, rnaseq? -->
Briefly, both UBF and c-Myc protein increased from baseline to week 3, however UBF content increased similarly in the old control, suggesting this was a general temporal effect rather than a training-specific response. On the contrary, c-Myc content was markedly lower in the old control group than in old intervention. Total RNA also increased in most groups including control, and differed by timing and not magnitude. The young increased primarily from baseline to week 3, and the old caught up by post, with no clear difference between age groups or intervention and control, and no volume condition effect. Lastly, the RNA-seq data revealed a largly age-independent training response dominated by up-regulation of ECM/collagen genes and down-regulation of RNA-processing/ribosome-biogenesis genes from baseline to post. The Age×time interaction is essentially null at the single-gene level, but GSEA shows old adults have a smaller-magnitude version of the same shared response (less RNA-splicing down-regulation, less angiogenesis/aerobic-respiration up-regulation). Training volume was impactful in the old (mitochondrial biogenesis up, contractile/translation genes down with more volume) but not at all in young. 

Findings from the present study suggests that ribosome biogenesis may be delayed rather than blunted in the elderly, as elderly reach close to the same levels of change as young, only at a later time point. The young group had the expected early rise following both moderate and low-volume exercise (19 and 16% respectively), which eased only modestly by post (12 and 11%), remaining clearly elevated above baseline rather than returning toward it — a pattern consistent with previous findings from our lab [@lian_glucose_2024; @hammarstrom_ribosome_2022]. While the elderly intervention group did not match this change after 3 weeks (mod = 8%, low = 10%), they achieved near similar increases at post (mod = 16%, low = 13%). These changes were clear across both volume conditions in the young at week 3, and for moderate-volume at post; low-volume in the young showed only a weaker, less certain trend toward an increase at post. In the elderly, a clear increase emerged only at post. Control also showed a similar baseline-to-post increase as old (13%), though this was a weaker, less certain trend than the changes seen in the trained groups. From baseline to week 3, the change in control was considered flat, at -1%. A possible explanation here could be timing of the strength tests, as post-strength testing was conducted three-four days prior to the biopsy - whereas at baseline biopsies were sampled before strength testing, and there were no strength testing at all around the week 3 biopsy sampling. Given that total RNA is quite sensitive to such stimuli [SOURCE ACUTE STUDIES], the strength testing alone may have caused the observed spike in total RNA in the control group, and does indeed present a methodological weakness of a poorly timed test. 

Changes in UBF and c-Myc protein matches the total RNA pattern quite well from baseline to week 3, with UBF tending to increase across all four intervention subgroups, albeit weakly, while c-Myc did not increase following low-volume exercise in the old intervention group. In the control group, c-Myc content decreased while content of UBF increased in a similar fashion to the old intervention group. Observed changes in protein content in the intervention group matches previous short-term/acute study findings [@figueiredo_impact_2016; @lian_glucose_2024], and the fact that low-volume training did not yield meaningful change in the old may further corroborate the narrative that increasing RT volume is more important for the elderly [@lixandrao_higher_2024]. What does not quite add up in this story, is the increase of UBF content in the control group, paired with a decrease in c-Myc, since UBF is expected to be a downstream and training-specific target, triggered by c-Myc's transcriptional control [@figueiredo_impact_2016].

The RNA-seq pattern observed in the present study quite closely matches previous findings. An earlier metformin trial in older adults found progressive resistance training to significantly increase expression of genes involved in ECM remodelling and down-regulate genes in RNA-processing pathways [@kulkarni_metformin_2020], the same two dominant, opposite-direction gene sets observed in the present study. Recently, an aged-muscle reanalysis across modalities found that combined training and resistance training were mainly linked to ECM, collagen, adhesion, basement membrane, also similar to our results [@yang_transcriptomic_2026]. Impaired transcriptional responses in mitochondrial, ECM and immune system genes have also been described as defining features of age-related anabolic resistance to resistance training [@deane_proteomic_2022], among these, baseline expression of genes related to oxidative phosphorylation was relatively lower in old compared to young, while genes related to activation of the immune system were relatively higher in the old, in the present study. The down-regulation of RNA-processing/ribosome-biogenesis gene categories at post compared to baseline may at first glance seem inconsitent with the increased total RNA from baseline to post. On the contrary, this fits well within the interpretation that once translational capacity has been built up, during the early-phase, further biogenesis-gene transcription is dialed back via feedback [@figueiredo_ribosome_2015; @hammarstrom_ribosome_2022].
